headline_marked: [[Cursor partners with Chainguard]] to secure open-source dependencies in AI-built code
headline: Cursor partners with Chainguard to secure open-source dependencies in AI-built code
summary: Cursor has partnered with Chainguard to route open-source dependencies through curated repositories, aiming to reduce the risk of compromised components in AI-built applications. This addresses concerns about trusting code generated by AI agents.
details: Following recent headlines about a potential $60 billion acquisition deal with SpaceX focused on training coding models, Cursor is now tackling the reliability of code produced by these models.

The company has partnered with Chainguard, a provider of verified open-source packages, to route dependencies through curated repositories. This aims to reduce the risk of compromised components entering AI-built applications.
This announcement comes as AI coding tools push more software into production with less human review, raising critical questions about the trustworthiness of the generated code.

Modern applications heavily rely on open-source libraries and container images from public registries like npm and PyPI, which often have limited security checks. Developers, and now AI agents, frequently install dependencies without full knowledge of their origin or integrity.

Recent incidents, such as the compromise of projects like Trivy and Axios in March through poisoned packages, underscore the significant supply chain risk. AI agents, making rapid dependency decisions, further amplify this exposure.

Under the partnership, Cursor users can pull libraries and container images from Chainguard’s repository instead of public registries. Chainguard's catalog includes millions of vetted library versions across Python, JavaScript, and Java, alongside thousands of minimal container images.

Chainguard employs a strict filtering process, building packages only from publicly available source code and avoiding components that rely on install-time scripts, a common vector for hidden payloads. If a package cannot be traced back to a verifiable source, it is not included.

The goal is to narrow the attack surface without disrupting developer workflows. Projects can be migrated with a simple prompt within Cursor, with dependencies swapped out seamlessly in the background.

This partnership reflects a broader industry shift in software production and protection. AI coding tools are now assembling full applications, including their dependencies, making the bottleneck not code writing, but verifying the safety of every component.

Without stronger controls, a single compromised dependency can expose sensitive data or halt development for days or weeks. Other companies, like Tessl with its security scoring for open-source packages, are also addressing this problem.

headline_marked: [[Benchmarked an LLM Running Entirely on a Phone]] (No Cloud, No API)
headline: Benchmarked an LLM Running Entirely on a Phone (No Cloud, No API)
summary: A developer built a custom benchmark suite for an on-device LLM, Gemma 4 E2B, running locally on a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra for PII redaction, bypassing cloud APIs. This ensures robust validation for real-world scenarios.
details: Validating on-device AI models, especially for sensitive tasks like PII redaction, requires more than manual spot-checking. A developer faced this challenge with their Redacto app, which uses Gemma 4 E2B on a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra.

Traditional LLM evaluation frameworks like lm-eval-harness, HELM, and BIG-bench proved unsuitable. They assume server-side inference, don't match the structured text transformation task, and fail to capture critical domain-specific behavior.

A custom benchmark suite was developed from scratch during a hackathon, designed to run entirely on the phone. This system includes dataset curation, a scorer, a runner, and a UI, all implemented in Kotlin.

The foundation of the benchmark is the ai4privacy/pii-masking-400k dataset from HuggingFace, which contains 17,046 entries with labeled PII spans. This dataset is crucial for testing context understanding as it's derived from real-world text patterns.

The dataset was meticulously filtered to approximately 2,000 high-quality candidates. Filters included length bounds (80-600 characters), a minimum of three entities per entry, and the removal of synthetic-looking names to ensure robust entity detection testing.
